name: The Arenbergpark Plane

location.address: Arenbergpark, near Kasteelpark Arenberg, Heverlee, Leuven

access: Free, open public park (KU Leuven's Arenbergpark, open grounds around the castle)
transport: Bus stop Heverlee Arenberg, short walk; roughly 20 minutes from Leuven centre
verify_notes: Onroerend Erfgoed inventory entry 309647 (Vlaanderen heritage inventory, 'vastgesteld' 2026-07-22): a solitary London plane in Arenbergpark, the landscaped park around the Duke of Arenberg's castle (now KU Leuven's engineering faculty grounds), possibly dating from the end of the 18th century. Already visible on a late-18th-century design of the park when it was laid out in landscape style (between 1775-1778 the park was redesigned in landscape style for the Duke of Arenberg). Measured girth 743cm at 1.5m height, crown diameter 34.5m, from the inventory's own 'Inventarisatie Houtige Beplantingen' woody-heritage survey (no survey date field given on this record). Age flagged: 'possibly end of 18th century' (mogelijk uit het einde van de 18de eeuw) is the register's own wording, a documented-period claim rather than a measured age; treat as roughly 230-250 years and say so is an estimate. Second source (KU Leuven's own heritage page for Arenbergkasteel) confirms the park's landscape redesign history but does not itself name the tree; count the register as the primary source and the park history as corroborating context, not a second confirming source for the individual tree, hence flagged rather than confirmed on the two-source bar. The park itself carries two protection statuses (protected village view since 1980, vastgesteld bouwkundig erfgoed 2021). Arenbergpark is open, unfenced parkland around KU Leuven's engineering campus in Heverlee, walked through daily by students and the public.

name: The Drie Linden Chapel Lindens
age_estimate: not documented; the chapel beside them dates to the late 18th century

location.address: Kapel Drie Linden, corner of Albert Woutersstraat / Panoramalaan / Kapellelaan, Wilsele, Leuven

access: Free, a roadside chapel on public ground at a street corner (a triangular public plot), always visible/reachable
transport: Wilsele-Dorp, roughly 15-20 minutes by bus from Leuven centre
verify_notes: Onroerend Erfgoed inventory entry 309644: three lime trees flank the small 18th-century Kapel Drie Linden (Chapel of the Three Lindens), on a sharp triangular plot at a Wilsele crossroads, opposite the historic Bleydenberg estate. Chapel presumably built last quarter of the 18th century by Professor Dominicus Jozef Hyacint Nelis, who bought Bleydenberg in 1773, in honour of Our Lady of the Linden ('Onze-Lieve-Vrouw ter Linde'); damaged during the French Revolution period and reconsecrated 1829 with a new Mary statue. Only cadastrally registered in 1865, owned then by the Wilsele municipality; the plot's sharp point was rounded off in a 1951 road adjustment, bringing the chapel closer to the street. No age or girth is recorded for the lindens themselves; the ensemble is the collectible point (the chapel with its three flanking trees), not an individually dated specimen, so age_estimate is left empty rather than guessed. Second source is a 2025 VRT news piece about the neighbouring Bleydenberg chapel/estate becoming a school classroom, confirming the site's public, roadside character and local historical standing; it does not itself measure the trees, so this ships flagged on age/species-detail rather than confirmed on every field. Species given as Tilia (genus) in the register with no species epithet; common lime is the usual planting for a Flemish chapel avenue of this date, stated honestly as an inference in age_estimate/species rather than the register's own word.

name: The Sint-Geertrui Wine Press Mulberry

location.address: Corner of Wijnpersstraat and Donkerstraat, a few metres south of the former Wijnpershuis of the Sint-Geertrui abbey, Leuven

access: Free, standing at a public street corner (Wijnpersstraat/Donkerstraat); the register locates it at the corner rather than inside the neighbouring school's grounds. The Wijnpershuis itself is now the Provinciale School voor Moes- en Tuinbouw (De Wijnpers), a working horticultural school; the tree itself is not stated to be behind its gate.
transport: Central Leuven, short walk from Grote Markt, roughly 10 minutes
verify_notes: Onroerend Erfgoed inventory entry 131504 plus its own legal protection decree (aanduidingsobject 944, definitief beschermingsbesluit signed 2010-07-12): a black mulberry (Morus nigra) at the corner of Wijnpersstraat and Donkerstraat, a few metres south of the monument-protected former Wijnpershuis (wine press house) of the Sint-Geertrui abbey (protected 1938), now home to the provincial horticulture school De Wijnpers (over 110 years on the site, per the school's own history). Measured girth 244cm at 1.5m height (survey dated 2013-10-23), short trunk (hoogte_stam 0.6m) before it forks, which is the species' normal older-age habit of leaning/sprawling rather than standing tall; crown diameter 17m. The register's own description says the tree 'forms a unity with the protected Wijnpershuis it leans on' (vormt een eenheid met het beschermde Wijnpershuis waarop hij steunt), so it stands close to the building. Protection covers a 20m radius zone around the tree. FLAGGED: single-sourced beyond the register and its own protection decree (both from the same agency, Onroerend Erfgoed); no independent second source found confirming existence, species or age. No age given anywhere; girth alone (244cm) is not enough for a confident derived age for a multi-stemmed, ground-hugging species like black mulberry, so age_estimate is left empty rather than guessed. The exact boundary between public street and the school's own frontage was not independently confirmed by a mapped photo; the register's wording ('op de hoek van' = at the corner of two streets) is the basis for treating it as street-corner public land.
